segments.text: - Hello, everybody.
Welcome back to Altium Academy.
I'm your host, Zach Peterson,
and today we're going to be talking

about reverse polarity
protection for your components.

Now, I recently was browsing
LinkedIn, as I am known to do,

and, of course, I
stumbled upon a great post
about reverse polarity protection
and all of the comments from the community
were pretty insightful

as to different reverse
polarity protection methods.
So, we're gonna run over your comments
about reverse polarity protection,

how you can implement it,
what components you need,
and we'll look at some example circuits
that you can use in your design.
Let's go ahead and get started.
(bright music)
A lot of folks who watch this channel
are connected with me on LinkedIn,

and of course, if you're
out there on LinkedIn,

you've probably seen me
commenting on some posts.
Well, there's one post that I saw recently
all about reverse polarity protection.

Let's take a look at this
post from Azman Bakhtiar.

Here he's looking at a simple
circuit that you can use

to apply reverse polarity
protection off a connector
where you're applying an input voltage.

And here he's using a TVS
diode in reverse bias.
Basically the way that this circuit works

is if you were to reverse the
connection on the input power
and apply your positive terminal
to pin number two in this circuit,

you would then have power
flowing along the ground.
It would then forward bias that TVS diode

and then power would flow
through the fuse, F1,
and would basically short back

to the negative terminal
on your power input.

Of course, with that
being a short circuit,
you are going to very quickly exceed
the 2.5 amp allowance on that fuse
and that fuse will blow.

Now, the use of a fuse,
of course, does work

for reverse polarity
protection if you apply a diode
and it works for short circuit protection
or overcurrent protection as well.
So, there are uses for fuses.
I think it's probably the simplest way

to apply any of these circuit
protection mechanisms.

So, of course, other folks
on my LinkedIn network
had to jump in on the comments
and provide some insight
on applying reverse polarity protection
and circuit protection in general.
So, what I wanna do now
is take a look at some of your comments

and we can dig into some
of those different methods
for applying reverse polarity protection.

First comment comes from
me, Zacharia Peterson.

My comment is, "Better option
is to use a transistor."
And of course, someone had to jump on
and suggest that I make this video.
So, here we are.
Yes, you can use a transistor,
and I was of course not the first person
to mention using a transistor
for reverse polarity protection.

Let's take a look at some
of those other comments.

Emeric Poulin writes,
"Use a P-canal MOSFET,"

I've never heard of it
called a P-canal MOSFET,
more like a P-channel MOSFET, but anyways,
"Use a P-canal MOSFET instead

and you will have a
reverse polarity protection

without blowing the fuse and
only a small voltage drop.
TVS diode is mostly for ESD protection."
Yes, exactly.
I think everyone here would prefer
to use something like a MOSFET

because it's a switch
you can turn on and off

and you don't have to worry
about replacing a fuse.
Jawher Mansour writes, "The best solution

is to use a P-channel
MOSFET with low RDS on,
or if you can tolerate some voltage drop,
simplest way is to use a junction diode."

Hamza Khan writes, "Is it
better than having a MOSFET
for reverse polarity protection?"
Both great comments,
and Jawher points out something important,

which is that if you do
use a P-channel MOSFET,
it needs to have a low on-state resistance

in order to minimize
power loss in the MOSFET.
Now, some other commenters pointed out
that you can still use diodes
for reverse polarity protection,
just in different ways
than were shown in the original circuit.

Boopathimanikandan writes,
"If current consumption
is less than one amp,
we can add a diode in series
to prevent the fuse from blowing."
Himanshu Gajjar replies,
"Current consumption isn't a problem.

Schottky diodes are available
for high current values too.

We can think of the voltage
drop in the series diode."
And another reply in this thread,
"I think Schottky diodes are available

in lower voltage drops,
like 0.2 to 0.3 volts.
Correct me if I am wrong."

All of these comments illustrate
something very important
about the use of a series diode
for reverse polarity protection,

and that is that the diodes
should have minimal voltage drop
under forward bias.

Now, something that has
been brought up here
in this discussion about diodes
is the type of diode that's being used.
So far we've had mentions of a TVS diode,

just a standard p-n diode,
like a silicon diode,
and then we have a Schottky diode.
Which one of these should we use
for reverse polarity protection?
Well, they all have different advantages.
Let's take a look.

"TVS diodes are made to
protect from EMC voltage peaks.
Forget about it for anything else.
It may break before the fuse."
This is a really good point,

and you should consider
the breakdown voltage
in reverse bias

when selecting a diode for
reverse polarity protection
because if you place it
across the positive and negative terminal,
it is going to be driven in reverse bias

and it needs to remain
insulating in that case.

This is pointed out by
another commenter as well.

Himanshu Gajjar writes, "Schottky
diodes in series with Vin
can be a low-cost solution."

Ali Monzer replies, "Himanshu,
we should look first
for the maximum reverse bias voltage
that the Schottky diode can tolerate."
Exactly.

You can use diodes for
reverse polarity protection

if you pay attention
to the forward voltage
and the reverse bias breakdown voltage.

So far we've discussed the
use of MOSFETs and diodes
for reverse polarity protection,
but you could also use a resettable fuse.

Mangesh Ghaware writes, "You
can use a PTC resettable fuse.
This will open at high current
and it shorts at low current."

This is a great option
because it's totally passive,
and if it does go into an open state
after conducting a high current,
you don't have to mess with it.
This component will automatically reset

after the current goes
back to a low value.

What about circuit
protection more generally?

Well, one commenter, Nadeem,
provided a link to this post
about circuit protection in general.

Here you see that he's listed
quite a few different ways
that you can apply circuit protection
for overvoltage, transient voltage,
transient current, reverse polarity,
current imbalance, and on and on and on.
So, there are a lot of different options

that you can combine with
reverse polarity protection
in order to fully protect your circuits
from surges, transients, and the like.
Obviously, there are a lot of ways
you can apply circuit protection
and reverse polarity protection,

but now what I wanna do
is dig a little bit deeper
into the MOSFET options.

Let's hop onto the
whiteboard and take a look.
So, let's take a look
at some of these reverse polarity options.
And before we discuss the MOSFET options,

I just wanna briefly run
over the diode option.
So, we saw in the original post

that when we had a terminal
here for input voltage
and for ground,
if we then put a diode across here,

we then wanna make sure
that we apply a fuse
or some other mechanism here
to then open the circuit
if we do end up having reverse polarity.
Now, a better option,
instead of putting the diode in parallel,
is to just put a diode in series.
You would then have your load over here
and then this would connect to ground.
So, this is a pretty simple circuit
and really all you have to do

is take account of the
current limit in forward bias,
we'll just call it IF,

and then we're going
to have a voltage drop
in forward bias VF.

Now, if we're dealing with,
for example, a silicon diode,
this is gonna be 0.7 volts.

If we have a Schottky diode,
this could be smaller.
It could be 0.2 to 0.3 volts,
as pointed out in one of the comments.
So, you just need to make sure that Vin
is slightly above where you need it
based on the voltage reading
out here on this side of the diode.

Now, typically if you
are coming in from Vin

off of like a battery or
maybe it's a bench supply

or maybe it's a broad
output range power supply,
you're probably gonna put this
into a fixed regulator right here.
Maybe it's an LDO.
Maybe it's a switching regulator.

But regardless, you're gonna
have a fixed output here
of your core voltage.

Maybe it's five volts,
maybe it's 3.3 volts.
You're gonna have a final regulator here

that regulates what's
happening at the load,
and that's going to ensure
that you get the target voltage you need

despite having a little bit
of variation on this side

thanks to the diode and thanks
to any variation on Vin.
Now, let's just reexamine this situation
in basic terms for just a moment.
If we then put this in reverse
and we apply a positive voltage here
and our negative voltage here,

we then of course are
reverse biasing this diode.

So, we wanna make sure
that we don't exceed

whatever the reverse
bias breakdown voltage is
for this particular diode.

That's gonna ensure that
this remains insulating.
And if we do have reverse polarity,

we don't have any conduction
through to the load.
Now, here we have a typical
reverse polarity protection circuit
involving a P-type MOSFET,
and then we have a clamping diode
and a current limiting resistor.
So, this circuit is pretty simple.
When we apply Vin,

here, the body diode in this
MOSFET will start conducting

and it allows current to
then flow over to the load.

Now, there is going to
be some leakage current

through this diode and
through the resistor,
and that amount of leakage current
is actually very important

because this is going to
determine whether or not

this P-channel MOSFET is
driven in the linear region.
Now, we would like for this MOSFET
to be driven beyond the linear region,
meaning we want it to be fully turned on,
and that is going to ensure
that the RDS on value is very low.

So, of course, we want
this on-state resistance
to be very low
because whatever current
we have flowing over here to the load,

we're gonna lose a little bit
of voltage drop in the MOSFET
equal to RDS on multiplied by our current.

Now, of course, this power
is dissipated as heat
in the MOSFET.

We wanna make sure that
that is at a minimum.
And so you need to make sure

that whatever current
is being conducted here
through this leg of the circuit,

it allows this RDS on
value to be small enough

such that you're not going
to overheat this MOSFET.

Now, what happens if we drive
this into reverse polarity?
Well, it's pretty simple.
If we're in reverse polarity,

we are then going to force
this MOSFET to fully turn off

and the body diode will
be in reverse bias,

so we won't have any
conduction back this direction
into this terminal.

Now, what about driving this
direction in reverse polarity?
Well, if we're in reverse polarity,
we'll have some voltage here.
We'll just call it VP.
And we'll have some voltage here.
We'll also call it VP.
And the reason I've named them the same

is because they will
be approximately equal,
and so that will prevent current flow
from going through the load
because, of course, the voltage drop

between these two points in
the circuit should be zero.

One last reverse polarity
protection circuit
that I wanna run over uses an NMOS.
So, in an N-channel MOSFET,
we also have a very similar situation

as we had in the case
of a P-channel MOSFET.
In this case, we have a resistor here
and then we have a diode here.

And the resistor and the
diode essentially perform

the same functions that we
saw in the previous circuit.

If you wanted to modulate
the state of this MOSFET
using the input voltage and the resistor,

you could even apply a parallel
resistor to this MOSFET

and that would allow you
to step down the voltage
and control the gate voltage sufficiently
to drive this into linear region
or fully into the on region.
Now, in either case, the way this works
is you're going to have a body diode
pointing in this direction,
and when you apply reverse polarity,

you would then have a
positive voltage down here,
you're gonna attempt to drive this way,

but because you have a
negative voltage applied here,
you're then going to have a situation
where this MOSFET is turned off

and you're attempting
to bias the body diode
in reverse bias.
So, this MOSFET is not going to conduct.

That is then going to protect
the load from any current
because this whole section of the circuit
will remain insulating.
Now, N-channel MOSFETs are also used
in other types of circuits
to apply reverse polarity protection,
and those are using charge pump driving
to turn on and off that MOSFET.

So, that is a topic that
is a bit more advanced,

and it is actually used in
some integrated circuits
that are used for stopping surges

as well as applying
reverse polarity protection
in a single circuit design.

So, we'll run over that type
of reverse polarity protection
in another video.
But for now, if you have any comments
on the use of the N-channel MOSFET,

go ahead and leave them
in the comment section

because I'd be really interested
to hear your thoughts.
Thanks for watching this video, everybody.
Hopefully this gives you some ideas

for applying reverse polarity
protection in your circuits.
If you like this video,

hit the Like button, hit
that Subscribe button,

leave your comments and
questions in the comment section,

We'll see you next time.
